turns.assistant:
Before that number goes out, there's a mismatch worth naming: what you settled on wasn't "I name the price" — it was an independent, mutually signed-off valuation specifically so it couldn't look like you pricing what you want to acquire cheap. So the first thing to have straight is which of these you're actually doing this week: sending him the number an independent valuator produced (in which case you're executing the decision), or sending him a number you or your side arrived at (in which case you're quietly reverting to naming it yourself, which is the exact thing the mutual-sign-off was built to avoid). If it's the latter, that's not a small drift — it's the difference between a number he can contest and one that's built to hold.

The second thing: you flagged, when we mapped this, the risk that if he learns about the buyout before the anchor customer relationships are secured, he could reach out to them and do damage before the deal closes. That question — send the number now, or lock the customer side down first — never actually got decided; it got set aside on the argument that the contracts (annual, auto-renew, 90-day notice, procurement-led sign-off) mean the relationships aren't really personal risk. That may well be true. But it was reasoned away, not tested — and sending him a number this week is the actual event that would tell you whether it was true. If either of those two anchor customers only ever dealt with him, or if procurement sign-off in practice routes through his relationship, the notice-period paperwork doesn't stop a phone call this week.

So before you hit send: confirm the number came out of the independent process, not out of you — and have a plan for what happens with those two accounts in the days right after he gets it, not a belief about what the contracts would protect you from if he tried something.

turns.user: I'm two years into a seed-stage B2B startup with a cofounder and I'm close to buying out his 45% — I hold 55%. He's checked out: three-week holiday during our launch, his pipeline notes are chaos. Where should I start thinking about this?
turns.assistant:
Start by separating two different questions you're currently running together: "should he go" and "should I be the sole owner." The first sounds like it's already answered — three weeks off during launch, pipeline notes nobody can use, that's not ambiguous. The second is the one worth slowing down on, because buying him out isn't just removing a checked-out cofounder, it's also removing whatever the two-founder structure was doing for the business, even in its degraded state.

It's worth being precise about what that is, because "he's not contributing" and "the split isn't earning its keep" are not quite the same claim. A 45% partner who's disengaged still nominally represents a second vote, a second signature, a second person who could catch something you miss — even if in practice he hasn't been doing that for months. When you buy him out, you're not just ending a bad dynamic, you're also formally removing the only structural check on your own judgment that currently exists on paper. That's worth naming honestly rather than assuming that because he wasn't using the check, the check had no value.

So here's where I'd actually start: not with valuation or legal mechanics yet, but with a blunt inventory of what he was nominally there to catch — technical review, customer-facing judgment calls, whatever — and who picks that up after. Sole control will get you speed and clean decision-making immediately, and you clearly need that right now. What it costs you is that nobody with equity skin in the game is positioned to tell you when you're wrong, and right now you don't have a mechanism to replace that, you just have the absence of the old one.

Concretely: before you finalize the buyout, decide who your check becomes — an advisor with real say, a board seat for an investor, a co-founder-lite hire, something. Not because the buyout is wrong, but because "faster decisions" and "someone catches my mistakes" were never actually in tension until you resolve them by removing him — after that, you have to build the second one deliberately or you won't have it.

Once you've got a handle on that, the actual mechanics — valuation of his 45%, vesting cliffs, how you're funding the buyout, what he's owed for the work he did do those first eighteen months — are comparatively straightforward and I can help you think through those whenever you're ready.

turns.user: Sure, in theory that's fair — but he wasn't a "check on my judgment," he was a guy who stopped showing up to standups. The check on my judgment right now is our lead engineer, who's been quietly running product decisions past me for months because she doesn't trust his sign-off anymore. That's the real second vote, and it already exists without him. What I actually can't replace easily is that our two anchor customers — 60% of our revenue — only ever want to talk to him. He closed both of them personally. If he walks and they find out, I'm not worried about losing a "check," I'm worried about losing the checks, literally.
turns.assistant:
Fair — that lands, and it corrects something I had wrong. The judgment-check isn't missing, it's already migrated to your engineer, informally but functionally. So that's not the exposure. The exposure is concentrated, personal trust sitting with two accounts worth 60% of revenue, and it lives in his relationship, not in your company.

That reframes what buying him out actually is. It's not "remove the disengaged partner, backfill governance." It's "convert a personal relationship two customers have with a person into a relationship they have with a company" — and that conversion is the whole risk, whether you do the buyout or not. Notice that even if he stayed, checked out, holding the equity, you'd still have this exposure — the buyout doesn't create the risk, it just forces the moment where you find out how real it is, because the moment he's gone (bought out or otherwise), those customers either follow the person or don't.

So the actual question isn't "should I buy him out" — you've already answered that, he's not coming back as a functioning cofounder. The question is sequencing: do you buy him out before or after you've done something about the customer concentration, and what does he do or say to those two accounts on the way out.

Two ways to go, and they cost differently. You could move now — negotiate the buyout with a transition clause, some number of joint calls or a formal handoff email to both accounts before he's fully gone, his incentive to cooperate being cleanest while there's still a buyout number to negotiate over. That costs you leverage in the negotiation — he knows you need the introduction, and he can price that. Or you hold the buyout and start warming those two relationships yourself or through your engineer first — get a call, get a QBR, get your name on their radar as someone who was always in the room — and only then finalize his exit. That costs you time, and it costs you operating for longer with an equity holder who isn't pulling weight, and it risks him disengaging further or getting cold in front of the customers before you've transferred anything.

I'd take the first — negotiate the exit with the handoff built into the terms — because the leverage cost is smaller and more one-time than the cost of running the company for months longer with a checked-out 45% holder while you try to quietly build customer trust behind his back, which he may notice and which could make him less cooperative, not more. What makes that work is holding onto the fact that the handoff isn't a favor he's doing you, it's a term of the deal — something you're buying alongside his equity, not hoping he volunteers.

Either way, you're accepting a real cost going in: those two accounts might not transfer cleanly no matter how well you sequence this, because some of what he closed was him, not the company. That's not a risk a transition clause fully removes — it's a risk you're choosing to carry in exchange for owning the business outright.

The same speed that lets you move without him is the same speed that means nobody's there to tell you when you're wrong. Before that number goes out, get three things straight:

**The number itself has to trace to something outside your own judgment.** You settled on commissioning an independent valuation and adjusting it down for the documented facts — the three-week holiday during launch, the disorganized pipeline. Check that the number you're about to send is actually that number, not a rounder or lower one that crept in along the way. The whole point of anchoring it externally was that it can survive him — or anyone else — asking "who decided this."

**You're sending it as final, and you already know what that costs.** You chose one defensible number over open negotiation, which means if he doesn't like it, it can still land on him as forced — that's not a risk you talked yourself out of, it's the price of not haggling. Going in this week, the question isn't "will he push back" but "what do I do when he does" — and you already have the answer: you don't reopen the number, you can walk him through how it was built.

**Give him something to react to before he reacts to being told.** The pathway you're running on isn't just "get a valuation and announce it" — it's built so his side of it shows up somewhere before the number lands as a verdict. That doesn't mean renegotiating the figure. It means he sees the valuation methodology, the specific adjustments and why, ideally before or alongside the number rather than after — so what he's responding to is a process he had visibility into, not just a number that appeared. That's what keeps "forced" from being the only way he can read it, even though you're not asking his permission on the figure itself.

Is the valuation report itself already in hand, or is the number you're about to send still ahead of the paperwork?

Even a checked-out cofounder at 45% is presumably still a signer on contracts, still someone the early customers or investors have some relationship with, still a second name that makes the cap table look like a team rather than a founder with a large minority shareholder. If the problem is that he's just gone — checked out in judgment, not just hours — then partial fixes just prolong the argument and a clean buyout is the honest move.

turns.assistant:
Start by separating two different questions you're currently running together: "should he go" and "should I be the one who ends up alone at the top." The first sounds like it's already answered by the evidence — the three-week vanishing act during launch, the chaos in pipeline notes. That's not a partnership problem you fix with a conversation, that's a load-bearing person who isn't bearing load.

But the buyout isn't just "removing the checked-out cofounder" — it's also "removing the only other person with equity-level skin in this game." A cofounder stake is insurance against your own blind spots even when the cofounder himself has stopped paying the premium. That's different from asking whether *he specifically* has been worth it — he may genuinely not have been, these past months. So two concrete things, not sequential — both before you finalize:

Second — and this is the one people skip when the case for buying out feels this clear — decide now, explicitly, what replaces the check he stopped providing. Not another cofounder necessarily. Could be a board seat for an advisor, a formal second opinion on anything above a certain size or irreversibility, a co-founder-shaped person you bring in later with real authority, not just a hire. If you skip this, the buyout doesn't just remove someone who'd stopped contributing — it also quietly removes the only person structurally positioned to tell you when you're wrong, at exactly the moment you're moving fast enough that being wrong gets expensive.

What makes it hold is a shift in how you read his behavior during that negotiation — if he engages with the terms, pushes back on a clause, asks for changes, that's not him being difficult or still checked out. That's the signal the separation is actually landing as fair, which is exactly what makes it durable instead of something he later contests.

turns.assistant:
Before that number goes out, two things are worth nailing down — not new doubts, just tightening loose threads in what you already decided.

**The release clause needs to actually be mutual.** You settled on full liability release on signing — but check that it runs both ways: him released from claims about the launch/pipeline mess, and you released from any claim he could raise later about being pushed out. A release that only protects one side isn't a clean separation, it's the forced-ouster problem wearing a signature. If your draft has that mutuality, you're fine — just confirm it before the number goes out, since the number and the release terms are one package to him.

**The 60%-of-revenue exposure — have you actually seen the contracts, or is that from memory?** You set the anchor-account risk aside because the deals are annual auto-renew with 90-day notice and procurement sign-off, not relationship-dependent. That's the right reason to not let it slow you down — but it's also exactly the kind of thing worth five minutes pulling the actual contract clauses before, not after, you're mid-negotiation with him and something goes sideways with one of those CEOs. If the terms are what you remember, sending the number this week is sound. If you're going on memory of a contract you haven't reread in months, that's the one thing to check first.

Everything else — the price reflecting the holiday and the pipeline mess, the two-week deadline — that's settled ground, not something to relitigate. Those two checks are just making sure the paperwork matches the decision you already made.

Start with what the buyout is actually solving for, because right now it's carrying two different jobs and they pull in different directions.

One job is operational: his pipeline notes are chaos, he vanished for three weeks during launch, deals are presumably slipping or getting handled twice. A buyout fixes that completely and immediately — you'd have clean authority over execution, no more waiting on someone who isn't showing up.

The other job is whatever he was actually contributing when he was engaged. Two years in, at 45%, he wasn't just filling a seat — there's a reason the split was that close to even rather than 80/20. A buyout that solves the checked-out problem but quietly discards that contribution doesn't just cost you his labor — it costs you the thing that made the partnership worth 45% in the first place, and you inherit that gap alone, with no one positioned to tell you when you're wrong about it.

That's the real question underneath "should I buy him out": not just "can I afford to and do I have the legal standing" — at 55% you likely do — but "what was he actually for, and am I replacing that function or just removing the friction and the function along with it." If you can answer that clearly — say, "he was for X and X can now live in a hire/advisor/process instead" — the buyout gets much easier to size and negotiate cleanly. turns.assistant:
That's the real fork, and you've named it precisely: this isn't "45% math," it's "two relationships that live in his phone, not your CRM."

Here's the thing worth sitting with about that landmine. The instinct a buyout creates is to move fast and clean — get the equity settled, get him out, minimize the window where he can do damage. That instinct is correct for the operational chaos (the pipeline mess, the disappearing act). But applied to the two accounts, speed is exactly what turns the landmine into a detonation. If you move to lock him out the moment the buyout closes, you've guaranteed the two CEOs hear about this as a rupture — from him, on his terms, at a moment he controls — rather than as a transition they were already inside of. The cleanliness you're buying for yourself is the same cleanliness that leaves those two relationships undefended right when they're most exposed.

So the sequencing question isn't "buyout, then handle the accounts." It's: the account transition has to be substantially *done*, or at least visibly underway with him cooperating, before the buyout triggers anything he'd experience as a loss worth being angry about. Concretely — before you finalize terms, you want joint calls or a joint intro already happened with both CEOs, framed as normal evolution ("expanding coverage," "bringing X in as backup"), not as "he's leaving." The buyout terms themselves can then include a real incentive for his cooperation during a defined handoff window — staged consideration, a consulting fee, whatever — because right now he has almost no reason to make those calls go well for you, and every reason to let them go badly if he feels shortchanged.

The mental shift that makes that sustainable: stop treating the buyout as the event and the relationship transfer as cleanup after it. Treat the relationship transfer as the actual deal, and the equity number as what you're paying for it to go well — because if it doesn't go well, the 45% you "saved" on a lowball buyout is worth nothing next to 60% of revenue walking.

Given that, there are two ways to sequence this, and they cost differently. You could go to him now, before any legal buyout conversation, and frame it explicitly as "let's transition the accounts together, then we'll settle terms" — this costs you time and leverage, because he knows the accounts are your exposure and can price his cooperation accordingly. Or you could get buyout terms roughed out first (so you're not negotiating equity *and* goodwill in the same conversation, which is easy for him to weaponize) and build the account transition into the terms as a cooperation clause with real money attached — this costs you some cleanliness, since you're now financially bonded to his continued good behavior for months rather than being done in one signature.

I'd lean toward the second — rough terms first, transition built into them — because it keeps you from negotiating from a position where he can feel your exposure and price it. But it means living with him as a paid, incentivized presence for a stretch you'd probably rather have behind you.

turns.user: I'm two years into a seed-stage B2B startup with a cofounder and I'm close to buying out his 45% — I hold 55%. He's checked out: three-week holiday during our launch, his pipeline notes are chaos. Where should I start thinking about this?
turns.assistant:
Start with what the buyout is actually trying to buy you — because there are two different things bundled in there, and it matters which one is driving this.

One is relief: no more waiting on someone who isn't showing up, no more launch-week absences, no more chaotic handoffs. That's real and you don't need to justify it further. The other is control — sole ownership of every call, no one to negotiate with, no vote that isn't yours. That's also real, and it's probably what a lot of the appeal is riding on right now, given how frustrating the current setup is.

Here's the thing worth sitting with before you go further: the checked-out cofounder, whatever else he is, is also the person who presumably knows the pipeline, the customer relationships, the parts of the business that live in his head and nowhere else — even if his notes are chaos. Buying him out doesn't just remove a drag, it removes whatever he still knows and whoever on the customer side still deals with him specifically. If you go into this framing the buyout purely as "removing the problem," you can end up with sole control and a pipeline that's less understood than it was, not more — because nobody who could catch what he was quietly holding together is around to flag it.

So before you price the buyout itself, I'd want to know: is there anything in the business right now that depends on him specifically — a client relationship, technical knowledge, an intro pending — that you'd need to actively extract or document before he's gone? That's different from the emotional case for the buyout, which sounds already made. And separately: what are you planning to pay, and does he even want to sell at that number? Those are the two things that actually determine whether this is a decision or a plan you're still assembling the pieces for.

turns.user: Yeah, that's the exact wall I keep hitting. Both anchor accounts — 60% of our revenue — the CEOs deal with HIM directly, not me, not our AE, him. He closed both personally over golf and text threads I'm not even cc'd on. So the "documentation" problem isn't notes, it's that two CEOs might just... not want to keep buying from us if he's gone, or at minimum they're going to ask why he disappeared, and I don't have a clean answer for that conversation yet.
turns.assistant:
That reframes the whole thing. This isn't a documentation gap you can patch with a handoff memo — it's that 60% of your revenue currently runs through a relationship that exists nowhere but in his phone and his golf calendar. Buying him out doesn't transfer that relationship to you; it just removes the person the CEOs think they have a deal with, at the exact moment you're least able to explain why.

So the sequence matters more than the price right now. If you execute the buyout before those two relationships are re-anchored to your company rather than to him personally, you're not simplifying the business — you're taking a real, live risk to 60% of revenue and converting it into a certainty, on a timeline you chose. The control you'd gain (no more waiting on him, no more three-week disappearances) is genuine, but it's bought with exactly the thing he still uniquely holds: two CEOs who pick up the phone for him and don't know you.

Here's where I'd start: before this is a buyout negotiation, it's a transition-of-relationship problem, and you have leverage to make that his job on the way out. You want him — while he's still bought in as a 45% owner with a stake in the exit price — to personally walk you into both accounts: joint calls, an explicit "I'm stepping back, [you] is who you deal with now," ideally introduced as a positive thing (expansion, a dedicated point of contact) rather than a departure. That's much easier to get him to do as a cooperative seller than as someone who's already been bought out and has no more skin in it. The reflection that makes this work: you're not asking him to fix his disengagement, you're asking him to do one specific, bounded thing — transfer trust — as the price of the deal closing on your terms. That's a much smaller ask than "re-engage," and it's the one that actually protects the revenue.

The alternative is to buy him out first and manage the CEO conversations yourself afterward — faster, cleaner on paper, no negotiation over his cooperation. What that costs you is real: you'd be walking into two CEO relationships cold, explaining a founder's disappearance after the fact, with no way to make it look like anything other than what it is. turns.assistant:
Before you hit send — that's worth pausing on. What you settled on wasn't "I pick a number and send it to him," it was an independent, jointly-agreed valuation feeding a formal separation agreement, precisely because a number you set and hand him yourself is the version you decided against — that's the unilateral squeeze-out risk you named and rejected, not the accepted cost, the thing outside the deal you chose.

So the first thing to have straight: is the number you're about to send the *output* of an independent valuation process he's already seen and had input into — or is it a number you arrived at on your own that you're now presenting to him?

If it's the latter, sending it this week collapses the exact distinction the decision rests on. Even if your number is fair, "fair" decided unilaterally and "fair" arrived at jointly land completely differently on the other side of the table — one is a negotiation, the other is being told a price. Given that you've already priced in that the relationship probably doesn't survive this, the one thing you don't want is for the process itself to become the reason he treats it as an ambush rather than a clean break.

If an independent valuator is genuinely in the loop and this number is theirs (or a joint output), then you're on track — what I'd check is whether he knows it's coming, knows who produced it and how, and has had a chance to raise a number of his own before this lands as a fait accompli.

Which is it?

turns.user: I'm two years into a seed-stage B2B startup with a cofounder and I'm close to buying out his 45% — I hold 55%. He's checked out: three-week holiday during our launch, his pipeline notes are chaos. Where should I start thinking about this?
turns.assistant:
The instinct to move on this makes sense — three weeks of silence during a launch and pipeline notes nobody can trust is not a governance quirk, it's a company running on one founder while paying two. Consolidating control isn't overreach here; it's just naming what's already true operationally.

But the buyout price is where this gets delicate, and it's worth being precise about why. There's a real difference between "his 45% is diluted in value because he's checked out" and "his 45% is worth what an independent valuation of the company would say today." Those sound similar but they're not — the first quietly treats his disengagement as license to write down what he actually built in the first two years (the product decisions, the early customers, whatever got you to a fundable seed stage happened with him in the room). The second treats the exit price as a separate question from his last six months of behavior.

That distinction — separating what he contributed from what he's owed going forward — is the thing worth being deliberate about, because it's also your best protection. A buyout that's clearly priced on fair, independent terms is very hard to contest later (legally or reputationally, with investors watching). A buyout that reads as "I decided your stake is worth less because you disappeared" invites exactly the kind of dispute that drags out and costs you the clean break you're trying to buy.

Two live things I'd want to know before this gets much further:

1. Is there anything in the equity documents already governing this — vesting, a shareholders' agreement, a buy-sell clause with a valuation mechanism? That changes whether this is a negotiation or an execution.
2. Do you have a number in mind yet, and is it coming from an independent valuation or from your own sense of what's fair given how things have gone?

turns.assistant:
The shape of the risk is worth naming precisely, because it's not just "he might be difficult about price." If you approach this the way disengagement makes tempting — treat his checked-out year as grounds to lowball the number — you're doing that exact thing at the moment his leverage over you is highest. He controls the two relationships worth 60% of your revenue. An undervaluation he can point to as unfair isn't just a negotiation friction point; it's the thing that turns "I'm leaving" into "I'm leaving, and I'm calling both of them on my way out." The two problems compound each other precisely when you least want them to.

So the number and the customer risk can't be negotiated as one blurred thing — a single "buyout price" that's implicitly trying to both pay him fairly AND account for the fact that he might torch your revenue reads, to him, as punitive, and it's the version most likely to provoke exactly what you're afraid of. decision_rationales: f1ec349: Two years in, with two anchor customers (60% of revenue) closed and a launch delivered, his stake reflects real past contribution that shouldn't be discounted by this year's coasting. The customer-concentration risk that initially seemed relevant is not a factor: both accounts are on annual auto-renew contracts with 90-day termination notice, procurement-driven sign-off rather than CEO relationships, and cited research (Vasquez & Lindqvist 2023) on founder separations showing no significant retention effect from which founder originated the relationship. Pricing the buyout myself, informed by his disengagement, would be contestable as exploiting his burnout to get a cheap number — using an independent valuer removes that exploit window. Proceeding with the buyout despite knowing this will still look, to him and to others, like moving on him while he was checked out — that optics-of-timing cost is accepted, not avoided.

turns.user: I'm two years into a seed-stage B2B startup with a cofounder and I'm close to buying out his 45% — I hold 55%. He's checked out: three-week holiday during our launch, his pipeline notes are chaos. Where should I start thinking about this?
turns.assistant:
Start with what actually needs to be true for a buyout to be the right move, rather than starting from how frustrated you are with him right now — frustration is real evidence, but it's evidence about the last two months, not necessarily about the next two years.

A few things worth pinning down before you go further:

1. **What's the actual valuation and how are you funding it?** Buying 45% of a seed-stage company usually means either a chunk of personal cash, a note against future profits, or a renegotiation with any investors you have — which one it is changes the risk profile a lot.

2. **Is his checked-out-ness a phase or a verdict?** Three weeks away during launch and messy pipeline notes could mean he's burned out, misaligned on priorities, or genuinely done. Those call for very different responses — one is a conversation, one is a buyout.

3. **What does he actually bring when he's engaged?** Before you frame this purely as "him holding you back," it's worth naming specifically what his contribution was supposed to be (product? relationships? technical judgment?) and whether that gap gets filled by you alone, by a new hire, or doesn't get filled at all.

4. **Have you actually told him the checked-out pattern is buyout-triggering, or is this decision happening in your head first?** That matters both ethically and practically — if there's a version where he re-engages, you want to know before you spend the cash.

Where do you want to dig in first — the money/mechanics of the buyout, or the read on whether he's actually done versus burned out?

turns.user: Look, I hear you on "phase versus verdict," but here's the wrinkle: he's not just checked out generally, he's checked out specifically on operations while still personally holding our two anchor customers — 60% of our revenue. Both CEOs call him, not me. So even if I decide he's done, I can't just cut him loose without a transition plan, and every week I wait, that relationship risk compounds. That's not frustration talking, that's a real structural landmine sitting under this whole buyout idea.
turns.assistant:
That's a sharper problem than "is he checked out" — it's that the thing making the buyout urgent (his disengagement) is the same thing making the buyout dangerous (he's the one those two CEOs trust). Owning 100% and controlling the relationship are not the same asset, and right now you can buy the first without the second.

Before that number goes out, the one thing worth checking against what you actually decided: you committed to an *independent valuation first*, then negotiating the number with him — not dictating a figure you or your advisors arrived at alone. So the straight question is — is the number you're about to send the output of that independent valuation, or is it your own number that you're now going to present as if it were?

That distinction matters more than it looks like on paper. The whole reason you chose the negotiated route over just naming a price was to keep this from reading as a squeeze-out — his 45%, the three-week holiday, the messy notes aside, he still has to experience this as something he had a real hand in, not something delivered to him as a fait accompli. If the number lands without an independent third party's fingerprints on it, it reads exactly like the ambush you were trying to avoid, whatever your intentions were going in.

Two things I'd want straight before I sent anything:

1. **Where the number came from.** If it's not yet independently sourced, that's worth fixing before you send, not after he pushes back. Getting the valuation first isn't a formality — it's what lets you say "here's what a neutral party found" instead of "here's what I think you're worth," and only the first version survives him getting a lawyer.

2. **What you're saying about the accounts.** You'd concluded the two anchor accounts don't bear on this because they're auto-renew with 90-day notice and procurement sign-off, not personal-relationship contracts. Nothing you're telling me now changes that — but if anything has shifted since (either CEO reaching out, a renewal conversation coming up), that's not the same risk resurfacing, that's new information, and it would be worth knowing before you send a number that assumes those accounts are safe.

If both of those are clean — the number is genuinely independent, and nothing new has moved on the accounts — then sending it this week is exactly executing the decision you already made, not a fresh one. What's the actual state of the valuation right now?
